body.en: Chapter 1 measured how \( f \) changes along the two coordinate directions. This chapter does two things with that: differentiates \( f \) along a path that moves through both \( x \) and \( y \) at once (the chain rule), and measures the rate of change along any direction at all (the directional derivative) — which turns out to be answered completely by a single vector, the gradient.

If \( z=f(x,y) \) is differentiable and \( x=x(t) \), \( y=y(t) \) are differentiable functions of \( t \), then \( z(t)=f(x(t),y(t)) \) is differentiable with \[ \frac{dz}{dt}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\frac{dy}{dt}=f_x\,x'(t)+f_y\,y'(t). \] Each term accounts for the change coming from one input variable, holding the other's contribution separate.

label.en: Worked example 2.A — Applying the chain rule

body.en:
For \( z=x^2y \) with \( x=t^2 \), \( y=t^3 \), find \( dz/dt \) two ways.

Direct substitution: \( z=(t^2)^2(t^3)=t^7 \), so \( dz/dt=7t^6 \).

Chain rule: \( z_x=2xy \), \( z_y=x^2 \), \( x'=2t \), \( y'=3t^2 \), so \[ \frac{dz}{dt}=(2xy)(2t)+(x^2)(3t^2)=2(t^2)(t^3)(2t)+(t^2)^2(3t^2)=4t^6+3t^6=7t^6. \]

Both routes agree.

The gradient of \( f \) at \( (a,b) \) is the vector \( \nabla f(a,b)=\big(f_x(a,b),\,f_y(a,b)\big) \). For a unit vector \( \mathbf{u}=(u_1,u_2) \), the directional derivative of \( f \) at \( (a,b) \) in the direction \( \mathbf{u} \) is \[ D_{\mathbf{u}}f(a,b)=\nabla f(a,b)\cdot\mathbf{u}=f_x(a,b)u_1+f_y(a,b)u_2, \] the instantaneous rate of change of \( f \) as you move from \( (a,b) \) at unit speed in the direction \( \mathbf{u} \). Taking \( \mathbf{u}=(1,0) \) or \( (0,1) \) recovers \( f_x \) and \( f_y \) as the special cases they always were.

value.en: \( \nabla f \) lives in \( \mathbb{R}^2 \), so everything from Linear Algebra Chapter 1 — dot products, norms, Cauchy–Schwarz — applies to it directly

label.en: It answers every direction at once

value.en: One vector \( \nabla f(a,b) \) determines \( D_{\mathbf{u}}f(a,b) \) for every unit \( \mathbf{u} \), via a single dot product

body.en: Which direction makes \( f \) increase fastest? The dot-product formula for \( D_{\mathbf{u}}f \) makes this a question Linear Algebra already answered.

label.en: ▲ Theorem 2.1 — The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent

body.en: If \( abla f(a,b) eq\mathbf{0} \), then among all unit vectors \( \mathbf{u} \), the directional derivative \( D_{\mathbf{u}}f(a,b) \) is maximized exactly when \( \mathbf{u}=\dfrac{ abla f(a,b)}{\lVert abla f(a,b) Vert} \), and that maximum value is \( \lVert abla f(a,b) Vert \).

Write \( \mathbf{g}=\nabla f(a,b) \). By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (Linear Algebra, Theorem 1.1), for any unit vector \( \mathbf{u} \) (so \( \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert=1 \)): \[ D_{\mathbf{u}}f(a,b)=\mathbf{g}\cdot\mathbf{u}\le|\mathbf{g}\cdot\mathbf{u}|\le\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert\,\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert=\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert. \] So no direction can push \( D_{\mathbf{u}}f(a,b) \) past \( \lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert \).

That bound is actually attained: since \( \mathbf{g}\neq\mathbf{0} \), the unit vector \( \mathbf{u}^*=\mathbf{g}/\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert \) is well-defined, and \[ D_{\mathbf{u}^*}f(a,b)=\mathbf{g}\cdot\frac{\mathbf{g}}{\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert}=\frac{\mathbf{g}\cdot\mathbf{g}}{\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert}=\frac{\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert^2}{\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert}=\lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert. \] So \( \lVert\mathbf{g}\rVert \) is both an upper bound for \( D_{\mathbf{u}}f(a,b) \) over all unit \( \mathbf{u} \), and a value it actually reaches at \( \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}^* \) — making it the maximum, attained exactly there.

label.en: Worked example 2.B — Directional derivative and steepest ascent

body.en:
For \( f(x,y)=x^2+xy \) at \( (1,2) \), find the directional derivative toward \( \mathbf{v}=(3,4) \), and the maximum possible rate of increase in any direction.

\( abla f=(2x+y,\,x) \), so \( abla f(1,2)=(4,1) \). The unit vector toward \( \mathbf{v} \) is \( \mathbf{u}=\mathbf{v}/\lVert\mathbf{v} Vert=(3,4)/5=(3/5,4/5) \) (since \( \lVert\mathbf{v} Vert=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5 \)). So \[ D_{\mathbf{u}}f(1,2)=(4)(3/5)+(1)(4/5)= rac{12+4}{5}= rac{16}{5}=3.2. \]

By Theorem 2.1, the maximum rate of increase in any direction is \( \lVert abla f(1,2) Vert=\sqrt{4^2+1^2}=\sqrt{17}\approx4.12 \) — larger than \( 3.2 \), since \( \mathbf{v} \) doesn't point exactly along \( abla f(1,2) \).
